choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.name: Choking in adults and children: what to do
choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.headline: Choking in adults, children and babies: what first-aid guidance describes
choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.summary: First-aid guidance describes back blows and abdominal thrusts for severe choking, 999 if the blockage stays, and a medical check after abdominal thrusts.
keyPoints: Mild choking is described as being able to speak, cough or breathe, and encouraging the person to keep coughing is the advice.
Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe, and the person may become unconscious without help.
For adults, first-aid sources describe up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts, repeated in turn.
Babies under one are described as having back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.
Anyone treated with abdominal thrusts or chest thrusts is described as needing a check by a health professional afterwards.

body.heading: How can mild and severe choking be told apart?
body.body:
First-aid guidance describes mild choking as a person who can still speak, cough or breathe. Such a person can usually clear the blockage alone, and the advice is to encourage them to keep coughing. The Resuscitation Council UK advises against blind finger sweeps of the mouth, because they can push the object further back.

Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe. Without help, the person eventually becomes unconscious. First-aid guidance only moves to back blows when coughing is not possible or is not working.

body.heading: What do first-aid sources describe for a choking adult?
body.body:
NHS inform describes leaning the person well forward and giving up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand. If the blockage remains, it describes abdominal thrusts, with a clenched fist placed between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, gripped with the other hand and pulled sharply inwards and upwards. This is repeated up to five times.

The British Red Cross gives the same order of steps for an adult: encourage coughing, then up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts. The Resuscitation Council UK 2025 guidance describes alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts until the choking is relieved or the person becomes unresponsive. For a pregnant person, the Resuscitation Council UK says abdominal thrusts are not performed, and the hands are placed higher, over the lower end of the breastbone.

body.heading: When is 999 called, and what if the person stops responding?
body.body:
NHS inform describes calling 999 if the blockage has not cleared, then repeating the back blows and abdominal thrusts while waiting for help. The Resuscitation Council UK describes calling 999 once choking has not been relieved after the first five abdominal thrusts. The British Red Cross says to call 999 if the person is still choking. St John Ambulance describes calling 999 or 112 for a baby or child if the blockage has not cleared. The wording on timing differs a little between sources, but each links the call to a blockage that has not cleared.

If the person becomes unresponsive, the Resuscitation Council UK describes starting CPR and making sure 999 has been called. NHS inform describes opening the airway, checking breathing, and starting CPR if the person is not breathing.

body.heading: How does choking in a baby under one differ?
body.body:
The NHS describes up to five sharp back blows, with the baby lying face down along the thigh or forearm and the head kept low. If the blockage stays, the NHS describes up to five chest thrusts, with the baby face up and two fingers placed in the middle of the chest, just below the nipple line. The NHS describes checking the mouth between each blow or thrust.

Abdominal thrusts are not used on babies under one year old. The NHS says to call 999 if the object does not come out, and to keep alternating back blows and chest thrusts until help arrives. If the baby becomes unconscious, it describes calling 999 and starting CPR. The Resuscitation Council UK likewise describes back blows and chest thrusts rather than abdominal thrusts for infants. The NHS also advises against finger sweeps, which can push the object further back.

body.heading: What changes for a child over one?
body.body:
The NHS pairs back blows with abdominal thrusts for children over one. It describes a clenched fist placed between the navel and the ribs, pulled sharply inwards and upwards, repeated up to five times, checking after each whether the object has come out. If the blockage does not clear after back blows and abdominal thrusts, the NHS describes calling 999 and continuing the cycle until help arrives.

The British Red Cross describes continuing cycles of back blows and abdominal thrusts until the object comes out, help arrives or the child becomes unresponsive. St John Ambulance describes starting child CPR if the child becomes unresponsive. For children, the Resuscitation Council UK paediatric guidance describes up to five back blows if coughing is not possible or is becoming ineffective, followed by thrusts.

body.heading: Is a medical check needed afterwards?
body.body:
The NHS says that even when the object comes out, medical help is advised, because part of the object may remain or the child may have been hurt by the procedure. The Resuscitation Council UK gives a similar reason for adults, saying that complications and injuries can occur after abdominal thrusts or chest compressions, so a healthcare professional should see anyone treated this way.

St John Ambulance says that every baby who has had chest thrusts, and every child who has had abdominal thrusts, should be seen in hospital, even if the blockage has cleared.

The Resuscitation Council UK published new first-aid guidelines in October 2025, so its current pages are the reference if details change.

travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.name: Which travel vaccinations might be needed?
travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.headline: Travel vaccinations: what the NHS says about which are needed and when to arrange them
travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS advises getting travel vaccine advice several weeks before departure, as needs depend on the destination, and some vaccines are free while others are paid for.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP practice, pharmacy or private travel clinic well ahead of a trip, because some vaccines need time to work or come as a course.
Which vaccines are advised depends on the countries visited, and TravelHealthPro lists the advice for each destination.
The NHS says some travel vaccines are free through the GP, including diphtheria, tetanus and polio, typhoid, hepatitis A and cholera, while others are usually paid for.
Yellow fever vaccination is given only at designated centres, is not free on the NHS, and leads to an international certificate.
Malaria is prevented with tablets rather than a travel vaccine, and the NHS advises getting advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before travel.
Pregnancy and health conditions can change which vaccines are suitable, so the NHS advises telling the person giving the vaccine.

body.heading: When should travel vaccinations be arranged?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP practice nurse or a private travel clinic well before a trip. Some vaccines need time to build protection, and some come as a course of several doses spread over weeks or months. The NHS travel vaccinations page gives around four to six weeks before departure.

Leaving it late is not a reason to skip the appointment. TravelHealthPro says some vaccines can still be given at the last minute, and malaria tablets can be started on the day of travel if needed. It adds that people who are pregnant or have a long-term condition may need to be seen earlier.

body.heading: Where can country-specific advice be found?
body.body:
Needs differ from one country to another. TravelHealthPro, run by the UK's National Travel Health Network and Centre, publishes country pages that list the vaccines and other health advice for each destination.

The NHS says a GP practice or travel clinic decides which vaccines are suitable and whether they can be given on the NHS.

body.heading: Which travel vaccines does the NHS list?
body.body:
The NHS lists several vaccines that may be advised for travel, depending on the destination. These include hepatitis A, typhoid, cholera, yellow fever, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, hepatitis B, tick-borne encephalitis, meningitis and tuberculosis (TB).

The NHS also lists the combined diphtheria, tetanus and polio vaccine among the vaccines relevant to travel.

body.heading: Which are free on the NHS and which are paid for?
body.body:
The NHS says some travel vaccines are free through a GP practice. These are the combined diphtheria, tetanus and polio vaccine, typhoid, hepatitis A and cholera.

Other travel vaccines are usually paid for. The NHS names hepatitis B, Japanese encephalitis, meningitis, rabies, tick-borne encephalitis, tuberculosis (TB) and yellow fever.

body.heading: What is the yellow fever certificate, and how is malaria prevented?
body.body:
The NHS says yellow fever vaccination is available only at designated centres and is not free on the NHS. It says the vaccine needs to be given at least 10 days before travel, and a checklist is used to confirm that a person can have it. A single dose is thought to give lifelong protection, and the certificate issued afterwards, the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, is valid for life.

Malaria is prevented with tablets rather than a travel vaccine. The NHS advises getting advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before travel, ideally four to six weeks ahead, though advice can still be sought at the last minute.

body.heading: What about pregnancy and long-term conditions?
body.body:
The NHS advises telling the person giving a travel vaccine about any health conditions or pregnancy, and bringing a list of any medicines.

In pregnancy, the NHS says to avoid areas where yellow fever is common where possible. It lists yellow fever among the live vaccines not usually advised in pregnancy, but says it may be considered necessary when travelling to areas where yellow fever is common, because the risks of the illness are so high. The NHS advises anyone unsure to talk to a midwife or GP about the risks and benefits.

head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.name: Head injury and concussion: when to get help
head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.headline: What happens after a head injury, which signs need 999 or A&E, and how concussion usually settles
head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.summary: Most head injuries are not serious, but the NHS says being knocked out and not waking, a fit or being unable to stay awake need a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says to call 999 if a person was knocked out and has not woken up, cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open, or has a fit (seizure).

NHS inform says to go to A&E or call 999 for repeated vomiting, a severe or worsening headache, increasing drowsiness or confusion; the NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if the person is being sick or feels dizzy.
NICE sets out when a CT head scan is advised in hospital, with separate rules for adults and for children under 16.
The NHS says someone should stay with the injured person for the first 24 hours; NHS inform describes a responsible adult watching for 72 hours when concussion is suspected.
Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness, and that going back to sport too early risks a second blow before the brain has recovered.

body.heading: What counts as a head injury, and what is concussion?
body.body:
The NHS says most head injuries are not serious, but it advises getting medical help for any symptoms. Concussion is a temporary brain injury, and the NHS says it can last a few weeks.

Headway describes concussion as the brain shaking back and forth inside the skull, causing mild damage. Being knocked out is not required. Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness.

Headway lists confusion, dizziness and forgetfulness after a significant blow to the head as early signs. It says headaches, poor concentration and sleep problems can appear over the following days.

body.heading: Which signs mean calling 999?
body.body:
The NHS head injury page says to call 999 if the person has been knocked out and has not woken up. It gives the same route if the person cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open, or has a fit (seizure).

The NHS also lists a fall from more than 1 metre or five stairs, problems with vision or hearing, clear fluid coming from the ears or nose, and bleeding or bruising behind the ears. NHS 111 Wales adds numbness or weakness in part of the body, and problems with walking, balance, understanding or speaking.

NHS 111 Wales also says that 999 is the route if someone cannot be taken to A&E safely.

body.heading: When is A&E the route, and when NHS 111?
body.body:
NHS inform says to go to A&E or call 999 for repeated vomiting, a worsening or severe headache, increasing drowsiness or confusion. NHS 111 Wales lists A&E for a person who was knocked out but has since woken, has vomited since the injury, has a headache that painkillers do not ease, shows a change in behaviour or has memory problems.

The NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if the person is being sick or feels dizzy. NHS inform says that when concussion is suspected but there are no signs needing urgent A&E care, it advises phoning NHS 111 for advice, even if a hospital visit is not needed.

body.heading: What happens at A&E, and who has a CT scan?
body.body:
In hospital, staff assess the person after a head injury. NICE guidance, written for health professionals, covers assessment and early management and sets out when a CT head scan is advised.

For adults aged 16 and over, NICE advises a scan if the score on a standard alertness scale is still lower than normal two hours after the injury. A scan within eight hours is advised for people who were knocked out or have memory loss since the injury, and for people taking anticoagulant (blood-thinning) medicines.

For children under 16 the rules are separate. NICE also describes observing children for a minimum of four hours when no risk factors are present.

body.heading: What about babies and children?
body.body:
The advice comes from local NHS trust leaflets, which differ a little. Many describe an adult watching the child for 48 hours after a head injury, while some say 24 to 48 hours.

The leaflets list signs for 999 or A&E, including repeated vomiting (more than twice), becoming drowsy or hard to wake, confusion, a fit, difficulty speaking or understanding, weakness in the arms or legs, loss of balance, problems with eyesight, and clear fluid from the nose or ears. For babies they add not waking for feeds, or crying that cannot be soothed.

Some leaflets put a headache that does not go away in the 999 or A&E group, while Alder Hey places it under NHS 111 or an urgent GP review unless it is getting worse.

body.heading: What care at home does the NHS describe?
body.body:
The NHS says someone should stay with the injured person for the first 24 hours. NHS inform describes a responsible adult keeping watch for 72 hours when concussion is suspected, and says the person should not drive, drink alcohol, take recreational drugs or play sport.

NHS 111 Wales says a person who is tired does not need to stay awake. NHS inform describes a staged recovery plan, starting with relative rest for 24 to 48 hours and light activity with little screen time.

Trust leaflets differ on timings, so the advice from the treating team is the one that applies.

body.heading: What if symptoms carry on, and when can sport resume?
body.body:
Headway says to see a GP if symptoms persist. One of its leaflets gives about two weeks and another gives 28 days, and it says symptoms that are severe or getting worse need prompt medical assessment.

Headway advises against returning to play or training until cleared by a medical professional, even if the person feels fine, and describes a staged return to sport. It says another blow to the head before the brain has recovered can worsen the damage and, on rare occasions, can be fatal.

NHS inform's post-concussion syndrome page describes pacing, which means increasing activity gradually, to help with returning to work and leisure.

heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.name: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke: what to know
heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.headline: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke: the difference, the signs, and when to call 999
heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.summary: Heat exhaustion usually eases with cooling and rest, while heatstroke is an emergency for which the NHS says to call 999.
keyPoints: Heat exhaustion can cause tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling or being sick, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin and cramps.
Heatstroke is the more serious stage, with very hot skin that is not sweating, confusion, fast breathing, a fit or loss of consciousness.
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving somewhere cool, removing extra clothing, drinking water and cooling the skin.
The NHS says to call 999 if someone has not started to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, or if heatstroke is suspected.
Older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions are described as most vulnerable in hot weather.

body.heading: What is the difference between heat exhaustion and heatstroke?
body.body:
Heat exhaustion happens when the body struggles to cope with heat. Heatstroke is the more serious form, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.

NHS inform says heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke if a person cannot cool down. The NHS says heat exhaustion usually improves once the person cools down within 30 minutes, and NHS inform describes it as usually getting better 30 to 60 minutes after cooling. Someone who has heatstroke, NHS inform says, is treated in hospital.

body.heading: What are the signs of heat exhaustion?
body.body:
The NHS lists tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling sick or being sick, and heavy sweating. The skin can become pale and clammy, and there can be cramps and a high temperature.

For children, the British Red Cross describes dizziness or confusion, headaches or cramps, sweating with cooler skin, a paler colour than usual, nausea, and fast breathing and heart rate. Its advice is to get medical advice even if the child seems to recover, and to call 999 if the child gets worse.

body.heading: What helps heat exhaustion?
body.body:
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving the person somewhere cool and taking off unnecessary clothing. It also describes giving plenty of water, or an isotonic sports drink or rehydration powder. The skin can be cooled by spraying or sponging with cool water and fanning. Cold packs wrapped in a cloth, placed under the armpits or on the neck, are also described. The NHS says to stay with the person until they are better.

The British Red Cross notes that babies under 6 months do not need to be offered water and may need to feed more often instead.

body.heading: What are the signs of heatstroke and what happens next?
body.body:
The NHS lists a very high temperature, and hot skin that is not sweating, among the warning signs of heatstroke. Others are fast breathing, a fast heartbeat, confusion, restlessness, a seizure (fit) and loss of consciousness. The NHS notes that redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

If heatstroke is suspected, the NHS says to call 999. It also says not to drive to A&E, and that the 999 call handler will advise what to do. The NHS also says to call 999 if someone with heat exhaustion has not begun to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled down and drinking fluids.

body.heading: What is done while waiting for help?
body.body:
The NHS describes cooling the person while waiting for the ambulance. This can mean wrapping them in a cool, wet sheet, fanning them, or sponging them with cold water. If the person loses consciousness, the NHS describes putting them in the recovery position. It also describes checking breathing and pulse and starting CPR if there is no sign of life.

For children, the British Red Cross likewise describes calling 999 straight away for heatstroke, moving the child somewhere cool and carrying on cooling while waiting for help.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk, and how can people stay cool?
body.body:
GOV.UK describes older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions as more vulnerable in hot weather. Conditions named include heart, breathing and kidney problems and diabetes.

NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance says some medicines may reduce sweating and affect the body's ability to control temperature, which can raise the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke. For staying cool, GOV.UK describes closing curtains or blinds on rooms facing the sun, and opening windows at night when it is cooler outside. It also describes planning activity for early morning or evening, drinking plenty of fluids, and limiting alcohol. Never leave babies, children, older people or pets alone in a parked car, the guidance says. Checking on vulnerable neighbours, friends and relatives is also advised.
